## Statement

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.
findings.used_clause:
is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.
consumer_premise_quotes: [F6] The canonical real square-summable sequence space $H=\ell^2$ is complete, hence a real Hilbert space. Positive-index coordinates are identified with the $\mathbb N_0$-indexed sequence space by the isometry $(x_j)_{j\ge1}\mapsto(x_{n+1})_{n\ge0}$. [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]] The set of finite-support sequences with rational coordinates is countable and dense: truncate any square-summable sequence so the tail norm is arbitrarily small, then approximate the finitely many retained coordinates by rationals. Hence $H$ is separable.

1.1 Let $H=\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$ and set $\tau_j^2=j^{-1-2\alpha}$. Each dyadic block $2^k\le j<2^{k+1}$ has at most $2^k$ terms, each at most $2^{-k(1+2\alpha)}$, so [F5] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2\le\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}<\infty$; here the geometric ratio satisfies $0<2^{-2\alpha}<1$ by [F11]. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$.
findings.soundness_explanation: The consumer uses the stated real sequence space and its canonical norm. Reindexing positive integers by n↦n+1 preserves every finite partial sum and hence the sum of squares and norm. Completeness therefore supplies the Hilbert target needed for the covariance construction. No complex or noncanonical inner product is inferred.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal basis of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$,
that is, a complete orthonormal family
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
define the **Fourier coefficient map**

$$\Phi:H\to\ell^2(I,\mathbb F),\qquad \Phi(x):=(\langle x,e_i\rangle)_{i\in I}$$with values in the space of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Then $\Phi$ is a linear bijection satisfying$$\|\Phi(x)\|_2=\|x\|,\qquad \langle \Phi(x),\Phi(y)\rangle_{\ell^2}=\langle x,y\rangle \qquad\text{for all } x,y\in H .$$

In particular $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete, hence a Hilbert space, with
the inner product of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

## Definition

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.
findings.used_clause: A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.
consumer_premise_quotes: The set of finite-support sequences with rational coordinates is countable and dense: truncate any square-summable sequence so the tail norm is arbitrarily small, then approximate the finitely many retained coordinates by rationals. Hence $H$ is separable.
findings.soundness_explanation: The consumer supplies the actual dense subset D: rational finite-support vectors. It is a countable union over finite lengths of finite products of Q and hence countable. Truncation controls the ℓ² tail, then rational approximation of finitely many retained coordinates controls the remaining norm. Thus D meets every nonempty norm-open ball, exactly the stated definition. The citation-title parenthetical changes none of that criterion.

## Statement

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and

consumer_premise_quotes: [F5] For every $q>0$, the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2qk}$ converges and equals $(1-2^{-2q})^{-1}$. [[thm-geometric-series]]

[F11] For positive bases, $a>1$ makes $x\mapsto a^x$ increasing, $0<a<1$ makes it decreasing, and for $t>0$ the map $a\mapsto a^t$ is increasing while $a\mapsto a^{-t}$ is decreasing, since $a^{-t}=1/a^t$. In particular, for $q>0$, $0<2^{-2q}<1$, because $\log2>\log1=0$ and $\exp$ is positive and increasing.

1.1 Let $H=\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$ and set $\tau_j^2=j^{-1-2\alpha}$. Each dyadic block $2^k\le j<2^{k+1}$ has at most $2^k$ terms, each at most $2^{-k(1+2\alpha)}$, so [F5] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2\le\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}<\infty$; here the geometric ratio satisfies $0<2^{-2\alpha}<1$ by [F11]. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$.

1.2 Put $d=1+2\alpha+2p$ and $J=\lceil\epsilon^{-2/d}\rceil$. Since $\epsilon^{-2/d}\ge1$, one has $\epsilon^{-2/d}\le J\le2\epsilon^{-2/d}$. The posterior variance satisfies $v_j\le\min\{j^{-1-2\alpha},\epsilon^2j^{2p}\}$. Therefore $\sum_{j\ge1}v_j\le\epsilon^2\sum_{j\le J}j^{2p}+\sum_{j>J}j^{-1-2\alpha}\le\epsilon^2J^{2p+1}+2J^{-2\alpha}\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}\le C_{\alpha,p}\epsilon^{4\alpha/d}$. The finite sum has at most $J$ terms each at most $J^{2p}$; for the tail, the block $2^kJ<j\le2^{k+1}J$ has at most $2^{k+1}J$ terms, each at most $(2^kJ)^{-1-2\alpha}$. The conversions between powers of $J$ and $\epsilon$ use the positive-base power order in [F11]. [F3, F4, F5, F11, given, construct, algebra]

The sum explicitly starts at k=0, matching the supplier and both dyadic tail bounds. Exponent laws identify (2^(−2q))^k with 2^(−2qk). No assertion about r=1 or the divergent branch is used.
